short.title_plain: Ramesses II Statues Found in Egypt
short.hook: A 2,000-year-old Ramesses II statue was found in Behbeit El-Hagar.
script: A 2,000-year-old Ramesses II statue was found in Behbeit El-Hagar.
Its head, 5.2 feet tall, wears the Double Crown and bears royal titles.
Experts estimate the full statue was 28 feet tall, based on proportions.
A second statue with a preserved face may also depict Ramesses II — not confirmed.
The site lies near a temple built 850 years later by Nectanebo II.
The temple’s dark granite structures date to the 3rd century B.C. and collapsed after Ptolemy III.
Could these statues have once stood guard over the temple?
Tap the link below for the full case file.
short.description:
Two colossal royal statues, possibly of Ramesses II, were discovered in Behbeit El-Hagar, Egypt. One has a confirmed head with the Double Crown and royal titles. Experts estimate the full statue was about 28 feet tall based on proportions. A second statue with a preserved face may also depict Ramesses II, though this has not been confirmed. The site is near a temple built centuries later by Nectanebo II. The ministry has not linked the statues to the temple. Source: Earth.com, https://www.earth.com/science/an-egyptian-farmer-reported-an-inscribed-pink-stone-on-his-land-and-it-led-to-two-statues-of-ramesses-ii/
Full case file: https://youtu.be/BDB2DcM3w14

Some visuals are AI illustrations.

fact_check: A 2,000-year-old Ramesses II statue was found in Behbeit El-Hagar. — The article does not state the statue is 2,000 years old; Ramesses II reigned c. 1279–1213 B.C., so the statue is about 3,200 years old. This number is unsupported and inaccurate.

The temple’s dark granite structures date to the 3rd century B.C. — The article says Nectanebo II built the temple c. 360–343 B.C., not the 3rd century B.C. (which is 200–300 B.C.). While overlapping, the 3rd century B.C. is a general term and not precisely supported. The article specifies Nectanebo II’s reign, not a general 3rd century B.C. date. This is a misrepresentation.

Could these statues have once stood guard over the temple? — The article does not mention any connection between the statues and the temple, nor any function like guarding. This is speculative and unsupported.
